opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the questions that really motivates a lot of my work. If you look at how a young child learns, they pick up an enormous amount about the world from very little supervision. Nobody hands them millions of labeled examples. A kid sees a handful of dogs and suddenly they can recognize dogs in all kinds of settings, lighting conditions, poses, even cartoons. Our machine learning systems, by comparison, have historically needed huge amounts of labeled data to reach that kind of robustness, and even then they can be pretty brittle.

The way I think about the gap is that humans aren't really learning each new task from scratch. Most of what we know comes from passively observing the world and building an internal model of how things work: objects persist, things fall, people have intentions, and so on. That background knowledge acts as a really strong prior, so when we do get a bit of supervision, like someone telling us "that's a dog," we only need to attach a label to a concept we've mostly already formed.

So for me the question becomes: how do we get machines to learn those kinds of representations from unlabeled observation? That's where self-supervised learning comes in. The goal is to pretrain on large amounts of raw data, images or video, so the model builds useful abstractions without labels, and then adapt it to downstream tasks with very few labeled examples.

One thing I've become convinced of is that how you set up that self-supervised objective matters a lot. Many approaches ask the model to reconstruct the input at the pixel level, but that forces it to spend capacity on unpredictable low-level details, the exact texture of leaves or noise in the image, that aren't relevant to understanding. Humans don't predict the world at the pixel level. We predict at a more abstract level. That's the motivation behind joint-embedding predictive architectures, where instead of predicting pixels you predict the representation of missing or future parts of the input in a learned latent space. The model can then focus on semantic, predictable structure and ignore what's noise.

We've seen this pay off empirically in label efficiency. Models trained this way can get strong performance with something like one percent of labels, or even a few examples per class, and they tend to be more computationally efficient to train as well. We're still far from human-level efficiency, especially in combining learning with reasoning and planning, but I think learning predictive world models from observation is one of the most promising paths toward closing that gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the gap is actually pretty striking when you look at it from a sample efficiency standpoint. If you take a child, by the time they're a few years old, they've developed a pretty rich understanding of how the physical world works. They know that objects persist when they go out of view, that things fall when you drop them, that a ball rolling behind a couch is going to come out the other side. And they've learned all of that from a relatively small amount of sensory experience, mostly passive observation, with very little explicit supervision. Nobody's labeling the world for them.

Now compare that to how we train our systems today. A lot of the large models we build, whether it's language models or vision models, they're seeing orders of magnitude more data than a human could consume in a lifetime. And despite that, they still struggle with pretty basic things about the physical world, basic intuitive physics, that a toddler just gets.

So the way I understand the gap is that it's probably not about the amount of data. It's really about what the learning objective is and what the representation is. A lot of our current approaches are trying to predict every detail of the input, every pixel, every token. And I think humans don't do that. When you look at a scene, you're not reconstructing every leaf on every tree. You're building an abstract model of what's relevant, what's predictable, and you're ignoring the rest.

That's a big part of the motivation behind the work we've been doing on joint-embedding predictive architectures, the JEPA family of models. The idea is to make predictions in an abstract representation space rather than in the raw input space, so the model can learn to focus on the predictable, high-level structure of the world and discard the noise. And when you do that, you start to see that you can learn useful representations from much less data, and the representations capture things like object permanence and rough physical dynamics without us ever telling the model about those concepts.

I'd say we're still far from closing the gap. But I think the lesson from humans is that efficient learning comes from learning the right abstractions, not from just scaling up the volume of data.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most striking differences is how much humans can learn just by observing the world. We don’t need someone to label everything we see, and we don’t need to try every possible action and get a reward to understand what might happen. We build up knowledge through experience, and then we can use that knowledge to learn a new task with very little supervision.

Machines have made tremendous progress, but they often require a lot of data or interaction to acquire capabilities that people pick up quite naturally. So the question, to me, is how we can build systems that learn useful representations of the world from observation. Can they learn what matters, how things relate, and how things change, without being told explicitly what to look for?

That’s a big part of the motivation for self-supervised learning. The goal is to learn knowledge that can be reused, so that each new task doesn’t require starting from scratch. I think that’s an important direction for closing this gap, although there’s still a lot we don’t understand about how humans do it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most striking differences is how little explicit supervision humans need. We learn a tremendous amount just by observing the world and interacting with it. A child doesn’t need someone to label every object they see or explain the outcome of every action. Somehow, from that continuous stream of experience, they build an understanding that lets them adapt to new situations very quickly.

With machines, we’ve made enormous progress, but we often need a lot of labeled examples or a lot of interaction to learn a particular task. And what gets learned can be quite specialized. So the gap isn’t just about how many examples you need; it’s also about whether the knowledge you acquire transfers to something new.

That’s a big motivation for self-supervised learning: can we learn useful representations from observations themselves, so that when we do have a task to solve, we don’t have to learn everything from scratch? I wouldn’t say we’ve figured out how humans do that, but it gives us a direction for making machine learning more efficient.
